lines: A log keeps flowing past, longer than anyone told you in advance, and there is room to keep only a small fixed slice of it.
The promise this topic has to keep is that every single line in the whole file ends up with exactly the same chance of surviving into that slice.
Whatever rule decides replacement has to work the same way whether this is the tenth line or the millionth.
answer: The reservoir size divided by how many lines have arrived so far is the only rule that keeps every line equally likely, and it naturally shrinks as the stream grows.

lines: Fill the reservoir with the first arrivals outright, no randomness needed yet.
After that, every new arrival draws a number across everything seen so far, and only a number landing inside the reservoir's own size causes a replacement.
Assume every earlier arrival was already uniformly likely to be sitting in the reservoir, and watch what one more step does to that.
Each survivor's chance multiplies by one factor for not being evicted this round, and multiplying all those factors together collapses into the exact same simple ratio every time.
A rule based on knowing the total count ahead of time cannot run on a stream that never announces its own length.
A rule that only ever looks at the first arrivals ignores everyone who comes later, and a rule that flips a fixed coin on every arrival favors whichever arrivals happen to come late.
Once the reservoir is full, almost every single arrival after it still has to generate one random number and ask whether it belongs in the reservoir.
At a huge stream length against a modest reservoir size, that adds up to a random decision for nearly every item that ever goes by.
The question is whether all of that random-number generation is actually necessary, or whether most of it is wasted effort.
answer: The number of items skipped before the next real replacement follows a predictable distribution, so that count can be generated directly instead of asking item by item.

lines: Instead of asking every arriving item whether it replaces something, compute how many items will be skipped before the next replacement happens, in one step.
Only the items that actually end up entering the reservoir ever cost any random numbers at all; everything in between is skipped without a second look.
Run both approaches side by side at the same huge scale and the difference in how many random numbers each one generates is enormous.
The skip-based approach's cost tracks the reservoir size times roughly the logarithm of how many times larger the stream is, nowhere near the size of the stream itself.
On a stream that can only be read one item at a time in order, skipping ahead in the random-number sense still means reading every item in between.
Only when the underlying source can itself jump directly to a position does the skip also avoid that reading cost, not merely the randomness.
A reservoir can also favor some items more than others by weight, but that single word hides a real ambiguity worth pinning down first.
answer: The weight that actually drives this construction is the chance an item wins at each individual draw, not the chance it ends up in the final sample overall.

lines: Give every item a uniformly random number, then raise that number to a power that depends inversely on the item's own weight.
Keep only the handful of items whose resulting numbers come out largest, held in a structure that always exposes the current smallest one for comparison.
Make one item ten times as heavy as four ordinary items and sample just two, and that one heavy item ends up included almost every single time.
The naive instinct of taking its share of the total weight and simply doubling it for two draws produces a number larger than one, which cannot be a probability at all.
Combining two separately sampled reservoirs fairly means favoring whichever stream actually contributed more items, in exact proportion to how many each one saw.

A real large-scale system's range partitioner keeps exactly that count alongside every sample it draws, while its simpler all-at-once sampling routine solves a completely different problem by counting first and retrying if needed.
Every item ending up with the same chance of survival, from a stream read exactly once, is what this whole topic has been proving one way after another.
The next question is not which items survive but what order they end up in, where every possible ordering has to be equally likely instead.
